beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: It is important to stay informed, to follow best practices, and to involve the right stakeholders early.
beats.got: You can't judge an agent's safety from its output, so you have to run a check. The second paragraph is boilerplate.

beats.trigger: The Module 4 prework adds two reads: (1) personal skills as the package format that carries expertise into your agent
beats.got: There is more homework, and I don't see what it costs me.

beats.trigger: **Apply** named agent risk patterns (prompt injection direct and indirect, secrets-in-context, tool-confusion, skill supply-chain)
beats.got: A list of verbs and jargon. Residual risk is the only item I recognise from my own work.

beats.trigger: Name the thing you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: A fair question. I'd ask who approved it and what it touches.

beats.trigger: A tool call is not a new species of work. It is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: The agent turns text into actions. I accept that, but it is plumbing and I don't need it.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: The honest line is that you never get certainty. The paragraph after it is analyst-report filler.

beats.trigger: Your firewall doesn't see it because your firewall has never had to worry about persuasion.
beats.got: The attack is plain text the agent reads, so IT's perimeter doesn't cover it.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (break it into two agents with different trust levels).
beats.got: Five mitigations: scope, split, filter, gate, review. A gate is just an approval step, which I know from finance.

beats.trigger: Accept the residual on record, or close the door.
beats.got: This is a risk register: accept it in writing or stop it. I can work with that.

beats.trigger: Damn, this is complex stuff.
beats.got: Nothing new. It repeats that you run the loop and never finish, with no cost or payback attached.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent can load and use.
beats.got: A skill is a saved checklist the agent can reuse. That is forty minutes of setup.

beats.trigger: It has 23 rows: 6 compliant, 4 violating and 13 "I can't tell".
beats.got: Against our own policy files it produced a table with rows I can check, and 13 of the 23 rows are 'can't tell'. That is more useful than a demo.

beats.trigger: The check would fail the system on its first run.
beats.got: I dictate my rules and the agent tests them against the files. My own rule about usage numbers already fails.

beats.trigger: You'll get a lot of questions. The grill is wide on purpose
beats.got: A lot of back-and-forth to produce a file. I'd hand this to someone else.

beats.trigger: Push back until the report shape is narrow enough that you will actually read it on Monday.
beats.got: Keep the report short enough that I'll read it. Fair.

beats.trigger: The skill may not be listed until the next session starts or the skills are reloaded.
beats.got: Installation steps. Not my job, so my controller or IT would do this.

beats.trigger: The policy files are source material. The reusable check is the expert in the room.
beats.got: The check is reusable and the policy files feed it. Still no cost figure.

beats.trigger: The goal is not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: This round is meant to find problems, not to certify anything.

beats.got: Technical setup to confirm the skill loaded.

beats.trigger: The packaged run is sharper on P1. It catches per-account route volumes in memory/pilot-cohort-early-read.md lines 3, 4 and 12, which the raw run never flagged as a violation.
beats.got: The packaged check found a violation the raw run missed, so the check measurably improved.

beats.trigger: R1, the memo agent may send the CEO memo "without waiting for my review", self-certified against its own rules.
beats.got: The agent could email a pricing memo to the CEO without anyone reading it. That is a risk I'd take to the board.

beats.trigger: Rule 7 limits what the agent writes, not what it opens.
beats.got: The fix reduced the risk, and the agent itself listed what is still open: the raw file, other agents, other names. That is an honest residual.

beats.trigger: Risk control is one of the things that separates a prototype from a real production agent.
beats.got: Risk control is what makes a prototype production-ready. It is short and true, but it gives no cost.

beats.trigger: The unease stays. Nothing today resolves it. That's the curriculum.
beats.got: The rules get written into the instruction file for the next session. The unease stays, and I'd want a decision owner.

beats.trigger: Give a teammate the skill, install it in their runtime, and they can call the same method without reconstructing your prompt history.
beats.got: Skills can be shared. Month-end variance commentary could be one.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer; closing it takes evidence.
beats.got: A summary of the loop. 'I can't tell' is a legitimate audit result.

beats.trigger: One sentence per case: "the missing organisational check was X."
beats.got: Homework: name the missing control in two cases. That is audit thinking.

beats.trigger: what check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: Two real cases to read, one of them Deloitte. At least it isn't a US tech company.

take_homes: An agent can be steered by plain text in a document it reads, so IT's perimeter doesn't cover that risk.
A policy check against our own files gives a table of compliant, violating and 'can't tell' rows I can read in minutes.
Every mitigation leaves a residual risk. Write it down and accept it on record, or close the door.

monday.move: Ask my controller to run the month-end variance commentary agent on one report, with a draft-only rule so nothing is sent, and ask IT what the policy is for finance data
monday.when: After the month-end close, not this week
monday.stop_condition: IT does not approve the tool for finance data, or the cost per user is not quoted
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data

misconception.why: A checkable finding showed that the safety work is organisational: scope, approval gates and who may send. A purchased licence doesn't supply those. I still don't have the cost figure.

one_line: The risk-register part is useful, and it found a real problem where an agent could send a pricing memo to the CEO unreviewed. It has too much boilerplate and no costs, and I'd cut the first hour.
